To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the asylum adjudication process is highly inconsistent; (2) the inconsistency is largely unexplainable by the factors that we were able to measure; (3) the inconsistency is not due to the fact that the asylum officers, immigration courts, and courts of appeals are not making their decisions based on law and policy; (4) the inconsistency cannot be attributed to differences in the types of asylum claims; and (5) the inconsistency is pervasive across all of the different adjudicatory bodies
the asylum adjudicators are inconsistent, that the inconsistencies are substantial, and that they cannot be explained by the case characteristics.

the asylum officers, immigration courts, and courts of appeals have very different approval rates, and that these differences are not attributable to differences among the asylum applicants, to the adjudicators' decisions in similar cases, to the adjudication process, or to the adjudicators themselves.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the problem of consistency in case by case adjudication.
the extent to which the asylum system provides equal justice for all.
the problem of inconsistency in the asylum system, and we believe we have identified a number of its causes.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

, at least as far as asylum cases are concerned, we should accept the fact that there will be a significant amount of inconsistency in adjudication and that the only way we can deal with this is by trying to make the process more fair, not by trying to make it more consistent.
the disparities in asylum approval rate are real, but that the disparities are neither as large nor as important as the study suggests.
, at least at present, the best we can hope for is a system that, in the aggregate, is reasonably consistent and that, in the individual case, is reasonably accurate.
